about: Radiation each mission adds, from NASA measurements, NASA estimates and NASA's own career limit. Doses are in millisieverts (mSv). 'kind' says what a number is: 'measured' (an instrument in that place), 'typical' (NASA's range for crews) or 'projected' (a NASA estimate for a mission that has not flown). The numbers are averages for the periods given; they change with shielding and with the solar cycle, and they do not include a large solar storm unless the text says so. Context for the crew: not a dosimeter and not an estimate of anybody's risk. Drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic). Same data as the technical modules (branch modules-en, data/radiation.json), with the profile ids of this app.

career_limit.what: NASA career limit for space flight radiation (effective dose), the same for all ages and sexes
career_limit.title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, career limit for space flight radiation, as given in the NASA technical brief OCHMO-TB-020

station.where: inside the International Space Station (NASA's range for crews)
station.measure: effective dose; about 40 to 90 mSv in a six-month mission

sources.short: NASA, Moon to Mars radiation protection
sources.title: Simonsen, Zawaski and Weeks, NASA, 'Moon 2 Mars: Space Radiation Protection' (NTRS 20250006168)

lunar_mission.measure: effective dose from galactic cosmic rays, NASA estimate (table 2 and section IV.C.1 of the source)
lunar_mission.note: Radiation: NASA estimates under 20 to about 30 millisieverts from cosmic rays for a lunar mission of 10 to 30 days (Artemis II and III), against a career limit of 600 mSv. The spacecraft is designed to keep the crew under 150 mSv in a large solar storm.

sources.short: NASA, Moon to Mars radiation protection
sources.title: Simonsen, Zawaski and Weeks, NASA, 'Moon 2 Mars: Space Radiation Protection' (NTRS 20250006168)

lunar_mission.short: Under 20 to about 30 mSv for a 10 to 30 day trip.

moon_surface.measure: effective dose from galactic cosmic rays, NASA estimate (table 2 of the source)
moon_surface.note: Radiation: NASA estimates under 100 millisieverts in six months on the Moon at solar maximum, and about 350 in a year at solar minimum, from cosmic rays. NASA's career limit is 600 mSv: at those rates, about 1.7 years at solar minimum and more than 3 years at solar maximum.

sources.short: NASA, Moon to Mars radiation protection
sources.title: Simonsen, Zawaski and Weeks, NASA, 'Moon 2 Mars: Space Radiation Protection' (NTRS 20250006168)

moon_surface.short: Under 100 mSv in 6 months, about 350 in a year.

deep_space.where: inside the spacecraft that carried NASA's Curiosity rover to Mars (2011-2012)
deep_space.measure: dose equivalent from galactic cosmic rays, average of the cruise
deep_space.instrument: RAD, the Radiation Assessment Detector of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory
deep_space.mission_note: NASA projects 1,000 to 1,200 mSv for a whole Mars mission.
